research_notes: Copyright registered 18 September 1899; contract with John Stillwell Stark signed 10 August 1899. Two copies of the score received by the US Copyright Office between 10 August and 20 September 1899. Originally composed for piano. A 1903 vocal arrangement ('Maple Leaf Rag Song') with words by Sydney Brown is a later adaptation, not the original work.

Year 1914 is the publication year (Pace & Handy Music Co., 11 September 1914). Reference recording used here: Bessie Smith with Louis Armstrong (cornet), recorded 14 January 1925, released 10 April 1925 (Columbia). William Grant Still arranged a version in 1916 while working with Handy. Widely recorded as a jazz standard.

original_instruments: alto saxophone | piano | double bass | drums
research_notes: Composed by Paul Desmond; recorded 1959 by the Dave Brubeck Quartet (Desmond, Brubeck, Eugene Wright, Joe Morello) for the Columbia album Time Out. Written in 5/4. Year is the recording/album year.

songwriter: Quirino Mendoza y Cortés (registered); lyrics drawn from older Andalusian coplas
research_notes: Year 1882 is the commonly cited composition/publication year of Mendoza y Cortés's setting (INBA, Spanish Wikipedia, Memórica). First recording 1918 per es.wikipedia. Several Mexican researchers (Arturo Ortega Morán, Ricardo Lugo Viñas, Gabriel Pereyón) argue the lyrics derive from older Andalusian popular verses (Sierra Morena, 'canta y no llores'); Mendoza registered the song. Attribution_type reflects that mixed origin. Later associated with mariachi singers (Pedro Vargas, Pedro Infante, Lola Beltrán, Vicente Fernández).

original_instruments: arpa jarocha | jarana jarocha | requinto jarocho
research_notes: Traditional son jarocho from Veracruz; verses are commonly improvised. Earliest known recording: Álvaro Hernández Ortiz as 'El Jarocho', Victor Records, Mexico, 1938 or 1939 (Wikipedia; Indiana University Cook Music Library says 1939). Ritchie Valens's 1958 rock-and-roll adaptation is a later version, not the original. Do not attribute authorship to Valens.

Written by Ian Tyson in 1961 (he later said ca. 20 minutes in manager Albert Grossman's New York apartment). Released September 1963 as title track of Ian & Sylvia's second Vanguard LP (album July 1963). Year 1963 is the release year. Canadian Encyclopedia: published 1963 by Witmark Music.
Published 1902 by John Stark & Son, St. Louis. First issued as sheet music, later as piano rolls. First known recording by 'the Blue Boys' in 1928 (mandolin and guitar). Originally a piano rag.

composer: Woody Guthrie (melody based on the Carter Family's 'When the World's on Fire')
research_notes: Lyrics composed 23 February 1940 in Guthrie's room at the Hanover House, New York, as a response to Irving Berlin's 'God Bless America'. Melody based on the Carter Family tune 'When the World's on Fire'. Originally titled 'God Blessed America for Me'. Library of Congress NRR lists Guthrie's 1944 recording. Year 1940 is the lyric-composition year.

Poem by Abel Meeropol published 1937, set to his own music; recorded by Billie Holiday 20 April 1939 for Commodore (producer Milt Gabler), after Columbia declined. B-side 'Fine and Mellow'. Pianist Sonny White improvised the long introduction. Year 1939 is the recording/release year. Holiday did not write the song.

Recorded 27 November 1936 at the Gunter Hotel, San Antonio; released May 1937 on Vocalion 3519. Wikipedia, the Discography of American Historical Recordings, and the Texas State Historical Association agree on title, composer, and recording date. Year is the recording year.

original_format: Solo piano with spoken dance calls
research_notes: Recorded 29 December 1928 in Chicago and issued on Vocalion 1245 in March 1929. Described as the first known recording with 'boogie woogie' in the title. The vocal is spoken dance instruction over piano. Year is the recording year.

original_instruments: Trumpet | Saxophones | Trombones | Piano | Double bass | Drums
research_notes: Composed by Billy Strayhorn in 1939 and adopted as the Duke Ellington orchestra's signature tune. First commercial recording 15 February 1941. Joya Sherrill's lyrics date from 1944; the famous 1941 recording is instrumental. Year is the composition year given by Wikipedia and PBS American Masters.

original_instruments: Trumpet | Tenor saxophone | Alto saxophone | Piano | Double bass | Drums
research_notes: Opening track of Kind of Blue. Recorded 2 March 1959 at Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York; album released 17 August 1959. Wikipedia and the official Miles Davis site credit Miles Davis. The piano-and-bass introduction on the album was written by Gil Evans for Bill Evans and Paul Chambers. Year is the recording and release year.

Monk composition, copyrighted 24 September 1943 as 'I Need You So' with lyrics by Thelma Murray. First recording was by Cootie Williams on 22 August 1944; Monk's own first recording was 21 November 1947. Cootie Williams received a co-credit for an interlude rarely used in Monk's versions. Bernie Hanighen wrote commonly used lyrics. NPR treats the composition date before the copyright as uncertain. Year is the copyright year.

Lyrics written by Thomas A. Dorsey in 1932 after the deaths of his wife Nettie and their infant son. The melody is Dorsey's adaptation of George N. Allen's 1844 tune 'Maitland', known with the hymn 'Must Jesus Bear the Cross Alone'. First published in 1938. An early recording by the Heavenly Gospel Singers is dated 16 February 1937. Year is the lyric-writing year.

original_instruments: Vocals | Acoustic guitar | Electric guitar | Bass
research_notes: Written and recorded by Johnny Cash in 1956 at Sun Studio, Memphis, with Luther Perkins and Marshall Grant; produced by Sam Phillips. Released as a Sun single in May 1956. Wikipedia and the official Johnny Cash site agree. Year is the recording and release year.

original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Harmonica | Piano | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Written by Willie Dixon and first recorded by Muddy Waters on 7 January 1954 in Chicago for Chess. The original single title on the label was 'I'm Your Hoochie Cooche Man'. PBS and the Library of Congress essay agree on Dixon as writer and the January 1954 session. Year is the recording year.

title_original: (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay
original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass | Drums | Keyboards | Trumpet
research_notes: Co-written by Otis Redding and Steve Cropper. Recorded at Stax in Memphis on 22 November 1967 with overdubs on 7 December 1967, three days before Redding's death. Released 8 January 1968 on Volt. Year is the release year.

songwriter: Al Cleveland, Renaldo Benson, Marvin Gaye
original_instruments: Vocals | Alto saxophone | Bass | Drums | Piano
research_notes: Single released 21 January 1971 on Tamla; title track of the album released 21 May 1971. Songwriters Al Cleveland, Renaldo 'Obie' Benson, and Marvin Gaye, confirmed by the Wikipedia song page, the album track list, and AllMusic. Inspired by a 1969 People's Park incident witnessed by Benson. Year is the single-release year.

title_original: Papa's Got a Brand New Bag
original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass | Drums | Saxophones | Trumpet | Trombone | Organ
research_notes: Written and recorded by James Brown in February 1965 at Arthur Smith Studios, Charlotte, and released as a two-part King single in June 1965. Wikipedia and AllMusic agree on Brown as writer and 1965 as the release year. Often cited as a formative funk record. Credited on release to James Brown and the Famous Flames.

artist: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five
songwriter: Edward G. Fletcher, Melle Mel, Clifton Chase, Sylvia Robinson
research_notes: Sugar Hill single released 1 July 1982. Writers on the Wikipedia infobox are Edward G. Fletcher (Duke Bootee), Melle Mel, Clifton 'Jiggs' Chase, and Sylvia Robinson. The Library of Congress essay states Grandmaster Flash did not perform on the track and that it was conceived and largely performed by Fletcher with Melle Mel. Year is the single-release year.

secondary_associations: Bonnie and Clyde (1967 film, later use)
research_notes: Banjo instrumental written by Earl Scruggs and first recorded 11 December 1949 in Cincinnati by Lester Flatt, Earl Scruggs and the Foggy Mountain Boys; released 15 March 1950 as Mercury 6247. Personnel on the original: Flatt (guitar), Scruggs (banjo), Curly Seckler (mandolin), Benny Sims (fiddle), Howard Watts (bass). Later used in the film Bonnie and Clyde. Year is the recording year.

Song by then-Princess Liliʻuokalani, dated 1878 on her manuscript at the Hawaiʻi State Archives, with Hawaiian lyrics and her English translation. Washington Place states she began it at Maunawili during an 1878 Oʻahu tour and finished it at Washington Place. The chorus mixes Hawaiian with the English lines 'One fond embrace' and 'Until we meet again'. Wikipedia notes melodic resemblance to earlier songs, including Charles Crozat Converse's 'The Rock Beside the Sea'. Country is the United States because Hawaiʻi is a U.S. state; the song predates annexation. Year is the composition year on the manuscript.

Bolero by Mexican pianist and songwriter Consuelo Velázquez. English and Spanish Wikipedia say it was written in 1932 and published in 1940. Indiana University's Cook Music Library says it was first recorded in 1941 by Emilio Tuero and Chela Campos, and notes a melodic relationship to Enrique Granados's aria 'Quejas, o la Maja y el Ruiseñor'. Year is the publication year. No single performer is treated as the original; the composer is used as the reference name.

Ranchera written by Fernando Z. Maldonado and widely associated with Vicente Fernández. English Wikipedia says written in 1972 and popularized by Fernández in 1973; Spanish Wikipedia says Maldonado was named composer of the year in 1973 for the song; Fernández's official biography places the song in 1976. Because those dates conflict, no year is stored. Attribution is to the songwriter, not to Fernández as composer.

secondary_associations: Also known as Camelia la Texana
research_notes: Lyrics by Ángel González (Estanislao Rivera Varela) in 1972. Popularized by Los Tigres del Norte on the 1974 album of the same name. Spanish and English Wikipedia and Debate agree on the writer and 1972. Year is the composition year stated by those sources, not the album year.

Written by Alberto Aguilera Valadez (Juan Gabriel). First released in 1984 by Spanish singer Rocío Dúrcal on Canta a Juan Gabriel Volumen 6. Spanish Wikipedia and the Library of Congress essay agree on the composer, the first interpreter, and 1984. The author has said the lyric was inspired by his mother's death in 1974. Country is Mexico as the composition's origin; the first recording artist is Spanish. Year is the first-release year.

Written and recorded by Stan Rogers for the 1981 album Northwest Passage (Fogarty's Cove). The original recording is a cappella: Rogers on verses, with Garnet Rogers, David Alan Eadie, and Chris Crilly on the chorus. Wikipedia, The Canadian Encyclopedia, and the composer's publisher site agree. Year is the album-release year.

Song by Leonard Cohen, first published as the poem 'Suzanne Takes You Down' in 1966 and included on Songs of Leonard Cohen, released 27 December 1967. Judy Collins recorded it before Cohen's album. The Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame and Cohen's official site agree on Cohen as writer and the 1967 album. Year is Cohen's album-release year.

Written by Joni Mitchell in March 1967. Judy Collins's commercially released version appeared in 1967 and charted in 1968. Mitchell's own recording is the closing track of Clouds, released 1 May 1969. Year is the composition year given by the Joni Mitchell Library citation of a 2019 Bloomsbury account and by her official site's March 1967 interview note.

title_original: The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald
research_notes: Written, composed, and recorded by Gordon Lightfoot after the sinking of the SS Edmund Fitzgerald on 10 November 1975. Recorded December 1975 at Eastern Sound, Toronto; single released August 1976 from the album Summertime Dream. Wikipedia and the Associated Press agree. Year is the release year.

original_format: Solo vocal with guitar and harmonica
secondary_associations: American folk revival | Peter, Paul and Mary (1963 hit cover)
research_notes: Written by Bob Dylan in 1962 and recorded 9 July 1962; released on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan (27 May 1963) and as a single on 13 August 1963. Dylan later said the melody follows the spiritual 'No More Auction Block'. AllMusic dates the release to 1963. Year is the composition and recording year. The Peter, Paul and Mary single was the main commercial hit.

Written and recorded by Dolly Parton on 22 May 1973 at RCA Studio B, Nashville; single released 15 October 1973, produced by Bob Ferguson. Wikipedia, the Dolly Parton Discography site, and NPR agree on Parton as writer and 1973. Year is the recording and single-release year.

Chicago house song written by Jamie Principle. Played from tape in Frankie Knuckles's clubs before release. First shop release credited to Principle on Persona Records in April 1986; a 1987 Trax issue was credited to Frankie Knuckles with Principle as songwriter. Wikipedia and The Guardian agree on the 1986 release and the Principle/Knuckles association. Year is the first commercial release year.

Issued under Derrick May's name Rhythim Is Rhythim on Transmat. Wikipedia's infobox, the Detroit techno article, and Roland's account date the release to 1987 and credit a piano sequence by Michael James. The same song article also says May followed 1987's 'Nude Photo' a year later, which conflicts with the 1987 infobox date, so the year is only partly settled. Frankie Knuckles is credited with naming the track. A later mix is titled 'Strings of Life '89'.

original_instruments: Synthesizer | Drum machine | Vocals | Electric guitar
research_notes: Cybotron single released in 1983 on Fantasy, from the album Enter. Composed by Juan Atkins and Richard '3070' Davis. Discogs lists the U.S. 12-inch as 1983, written by 3070 and Juan Atkins. Recorded April 1982 according to the song article. Year is the release year. John Housely played guitar on the album.

title_english: The Snap Beans Are Not Salty
research_notes: 1965 Arhoolie single 'Zydeco Et Pas Sale', also spelled 'Zydeco Sont Pas Salé'. Smithsonian Folkways traces the phrase 'les haricots sont pas salés' to Creole dance-song tradition and notes a 1934 John and Alan Lomax field recording of the line. Chenier's 1965 version, recorded with Chris Strachwitz, is the reference recording. Year is Chenier's recording year, not the traditional origin. Genre name Zydeco is not yet in the taxonomy.

Written by Sam Cooke and recorded 30 January 1964 at RCA in Hollywood. Album track on Ain't That Good News (February 1964); single released 22 December 1964, after Cooke's death on 11 December 1964. The Songwriters Hall of Fame says it was written in 1963 and recorded in January 1964. Produced by Hugo & Luigi, arranged by René Hall. Year is the recording and release year.

original_instruments: Vocals | Clavinet | Drums | Moog bass | Tenor saxophone | Trumpet
research_notes: Written by Stevie Wonder and released in 1972 as the lead single from Talking Book, recorded at Electric Lady Studios, New York. Wikipedia and BBC Radio 2 credit Wonder. A version was also intended for Jeff Beck. Wonder plays clavinet, drums, and Moog bass on the issued track. Year is the release year. The Wikipedia infobox says November 1972; the article body also gives a single date of 24 October 1972.

original_format: Vocal with electric guitar and rhythm section
original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Piano | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Written and sung by Chuck Berry, Chess single released 31 March 1958. Wikipedia says recorded 6 January 1958; the Discography of American Historical Recordings dates the Chess master to February 1958 in Chicago, with Lafayette Leake (piano), Willie Dixon (bass), and Fred Below (drums). The release year 1958 is consistent. Wikipedia also says Berry wrote the song in 1955. Year is the release year.

composer: James Hetfield, Lars Ulrich, Cliff Burton, Kirk Hammett
research_notes: Title track of Metallica's album Master of Puppets, released 3 March 1986; the song was issued as a single on 2 July 1986. Music credited to James Hetfield, Lars Ulrich, Cliff Burton, and Kirk Hammett; lyrics by Hetfield. Recorded October–December 1985 at Sweet Silence Studios, Copenhagen. The official Metallica site confirms the album date and track. Year is the album-release year.

original_instruments: Vocals | Guitar | Harmonica | Pedal steel guitar | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Written by Neil Young. Recorded 6–8 February 1971 at Quadrafonic Sound, Nashville, with Linda Ronstadt and James Taylor on backing vocals; U.S. single released January 1972 from the album Harvest (15 February 1972). Wikipedia calls Young a Canadian singer-songwriter. Year is the single-release year.

secondary_associations: Later widely known through covers and the film Shrek
research_notes: Written by Leonard Cohen and released on Various Positions. Official site dates the album 11 December 1984 and lists Hallelujah as track 5. Recorded June 1984. The Canadian Encyclopedia discusses the song as Cohen's. A later John Cale version was used in Shrek; the song was not written for that film. Year is the album-release year.

Written by Jimi Hendrix. UK single released 17 March 1967 on Track; basic track recorded 11 January 1967 at De Lane Lea, London, with overdubs at Olympic in February 1967. The official Hendrix site confirms the 17 March 1967 UK single. Country is the United States as Hendrix's origin; the recording was made in London. Year is the UK release year.

original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass | Drums | Piano | Organ | Saxophones | Trumpet
research_notes: Otis Redding single from Otis Blue, released August 1965 according to the Wikipedia infobox; the Library of Congress essay calls it Redding's original composition on Stax in 1965. Wikipedia also reports a conflicting account that Earl Sims brought an earlier version and that authorship was disputed. Aretha Franklin's 1967 recording is a later cover. Year is the 1965 release year. Verification is partial because of the authorship dispute.

title_english: The Son of the Black Woman
secondary_associations: Jalisco | Nayarit | Blas Galindo (1940 orchestral arrangement)
research_notes: Traditional son of western Mexico, widely used as a mariachi entrance piece. Spanish Wikipedia and Jesús Jáuregui's INAH research treat it as collectively transmitted, not the work of one author; a 1925 printed reference and recordings from 1929 and 1937 are cited. English Wikipedia's infobox credits Blas Galindo and a 1940 release, which describes his concert arrangement in Sones de mariachi rather than the folk son. No composition year is stored. Galindo's orchestral suite is a separate concert work.

Second single from Selena's album Entre a Mi Mundo, released October 1992 on EMI Latin. English Wikipedia and Wikidata credit A. B. Quintanilla and Pete Astudillo and give the United States as country of origin. The Spanish Wikipedia infobox also lists Selena Quintanilla, Ricky Vela, and Sammy Morales among the authors, so the full credit line is not settled here. Year is the single-release year.

Opening song of Buffy Sainte-Marie's debut album It's My Way!, released April 1964 on Vanguard. Wikipedia and The Canadian Encyclopedia describe it as her protest song about the taking of Indigenous land, including the Kinzua Dam and the Treaty of Canandaigua. Arrangement on the album is vocal, guitar, and Art Davis on bass. Year is the album-release year.

original_instruments: Tenor saxophone | Piano | Double bass | Drums
research_notes: Jazz composition by John Coltrane, recorded May 1959 at Atlantic Studios, New York, and released on the album Giant Steps in February 1960. The Library of Congress essay and the composition article agree. The chord cycle is known as Coltrane changes. Year is the recording year.

original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass | Drums | Piano | Saxophone
research_notes: Written by Bruce Springsteen. Single and album released 25 August 1975 on Columbia. The song was recorded between January and August 1974 at 914 Sound Studios, Blauvelt, New York. AllMusic dates the album 25 August 1975. Year is the release year.

composer: Kurt Cobain, Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic
research_notes: Lead single from Nirvana's album Nevermind, released 10 September 1991. Recorded May 1991 at Sound City, Van Nuys. Music credited to Kurt Cobain, Dave Grohl, and Krist Novoselic; lyrics by Cobain. AllMusic and HISTORY.com agree on the 1991 release and the three composers. Year is the single-release year.

Written by Michael Jackson. Recorded in 1982 at Westlake, Los Angeles, for the album Thriller (29 November 1982). Single released 2 January 1983 according to the song article; the album article says 3 January 1983. AllMusic lists the song's release year as 1982, matching the album. Year stored is the single-release year 1983. Produced by Quincy Jones and Jackson.

songwriter: Sylvia Robinson, Henry Jackson, Michael Wright, Guy O'Brien
original_format: Rap over a played rhythm track
secondary_associations: Sugar Hill Records | Interpolation of Chic's Good Times
research_notes: Debut single of the Sugarhill Gang, produced by Sylvia Robinson, released 16 September 1979 and recorded 2 August 1979. The track uses the bass line of Chic's 'Good Times'; Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards received songwriting credits after a settlement. The Guardian interview with the group and the Library of Congress essay agree on the 1979 Sugarhill release. Year is the release year.

Edwin Hawkins's gospel arrangement of the hymn 'Oh Happy Day', whose text is by Philip Doddridge. Recorded in 1967 at the Ephesian Church of God in Christ, Berkeley, with Dorothy Combs Morrison as lead singer, and issued as a U.S. single in April 1969. Official Charts shows the UK chart run beginning 27 May 1969. Year is the U.S. single-release year. Hawkins is credited as arranger and pianist.

secondary_associations: Oaxaca | Isthmus of Tehuantepec | Chavela Vargas (later well-known recording)
research_notes: Mexican folk song from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, in son istmeño style. Spanish Wikipedia and a Library of Congress folklife essay say there is no single text or known author; early printed versions are cited from the 1930s, and Andrés Henestrosa helped circulate it. Common later recordings include Chavela Vargas. No composition year is stored. Genre name Son istmeño is not yet in the taxonomy.

Lyrics by Gilles Vigneault; music co-written with Gaston Rochon. First sung at the 1975 Fête nationale on Mount Royal, Montreal. French Wikipedia dates a manuscript 15 May 1975 and a first performance on 20 June 1975; the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Montreal Fête nationale site say the public premiere was 24 June 1975. Year 1975 is agreed. Not the same song as Vigneault's 'Les gens de mon pays'.

songwriter: Al Green, Willie Mitchell, Al Jackson Jr.
research_notes: Single released November 1971 on Hi 2202; the album Let's Stay Together followed on 31 January 1972. Songwriters Al Green, Willie Mitchell, and Al Jackson Jr.; produced by Mitchell at Royal Studios, Memphis. Wikipedia and the Library of Congress essay agree. Year is the single-release year. The album page gives December 1971 for the single, a one-month difference from the song page.

songwriter: Ben E. King, Jerry Leiber, Mike Stoller
secondary_associations: Later used in the 1986 film Stand by Me
research_notes: Recorded by Ben E. King on 27 October 1960 and released in 1961 on Atco. Written by King with Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, who were credited on the original single under the pseudonym Elmo Glick. King said the title was inspired by a Soul Stirrers spiritual. The Songwriters Hall of Fame agrees on the three writers and the 1961 hit. The 1986 film use came later. Year is the release year.

songwriter: George Clinton, Bootsy Collins, Bernie Worrell
research_notes: Parliament single released 28 January 1978 from the 1977 album Funkentelechy vs. the Placebo Syndrome. Written by George Clinton, Bootsy Collins, and Bernie Worrell. The bass line on the record was played by Worrell on Minimoog after Collins rejected the part. Both Wikipedia pages agree. Year is the single-release year.

title_english: Move Your Body (The House Music Anthem)
research_notes: Chicago house track released by Trax in June 1986 as TX117, subtitled The House Music Anthem. Writing credit on the record is Virgo, Jefferson's alias. Lead vocal by Curtis McClain, often uncredited on the label. Circulated on cassette in Chicago clubs in 1985 before release. Wikipedia, Trax Records, and Rolling Stone Australia agree on Jefferson, Trax, and 1986. Piano is part of the recording; a separate published piano score was not found. Year is the release year.

Ranchera written and released by José Alfredo Jiménez in 1971, from the album El Rey. English and Spanish Wikipedia and El Universal agree on Jiménez as author and 1971. Vicente Fernández's 1973 recording is a later version. Year is the Jiménez release year.

Bolero by Mexican composer Álvaro Carrillo. Spanish Wikipedia says he registered it on 11 July 1958 and it was first recorded in 1959, becoming Mexico's most successful song of 1960. Early recordings include Los Tres Ases and Rolando Laserie. The Originals database lists Tres Ases, RCA Victor, 1959, author Carrillo. Year is the first-recording year. The composer is used as the reference name because several artists recorded it at the start.

songwriter: Rob Baker, Gordon Downie, Johnny Fay, Paul Langlois, Gord Sinclair
research_notes: Lead single from The Tragically Hip's album Trouble at the Henhouse, released 22 April 1996. Songwriters credited as Rob Baker, Gordon Downie, Johnny Fay, Paul Langlois, and Gord Sinclair. The album page says all songs were written by the band. Year is the single-release year.

songwriter: Abel Tesfaye, Ahmad Balshe, Jason Quenneville, Max Martin, Oscar Holter
research_notes: Single by Canadian singer The Weeknd (Abel Tesfaye), released 29 November 2019, later on the album After Hours (20 March 2020). Writers: Tesfaye, Ahmad Balshe, Jason Quenneville, Max Martin, and Oscar Holter. Produced by Max Martin, Oscar Holter, and The Weeknd. Official Charts shows a UK chart entry from 12 December 2019. Year is the single-release year.

Written by Willie Nelson and recorded by Patsy Cline. The Library of Congress essay says the band track was recorded on 21 August 1961 and Cline completed her vocal a few days later. Wikipedia says Decca released the single in October 1961. Produced by Owen Bradley. Year is the release year.

artist: Bill Monroe and His Blue Grass Boys
original_instruments: Vocals | Mandolin | Guitar | Banjo | Fiddle | Bass
research_notes: Waltz written by Bill Monroe. Wikipedia and the Library of Congress essay say the earliest known performance was on the Grand Ole Opry on 25 August 1945, and the Columbia recording was made on 16 September 1946 in Chicago. The Discography of American Historical Recordings lists the same take date. Wikipedia says that recording was released in early 1947. The session included Lester Flatt and Earl Scruggs. Year is the recording year. Elvis Presley's 1954 version is a later cover.

songwriter: Berry Gordy, Freddie Perren, Alphonso Mizell, Deke Richards
research_notes: First Motown single by the Jackson 5, from Diana Ross Presents The Jackson 5. Written and produced by The Corporation: Berry Gordy, Freddie Perren, Alphonso Mizell, and Deke Richards. Wikipedia, Classic Motown, and AllMusic agree on the writers and a 1969 release. The song page gives 7 October 1969 and also mentions 6 October 1969; the album page and Motown give 7 October. Year is 1969.

original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass | Drums | Piano
research_notes: Chic single released 21 September 1978 from the album C'est Chic, written and produced by Bernard Edwards and Nile Rodgers. Recorded January 1978 at Power Station, New York. Official Charts lists a UK chart entry from 18 November 1978. Piano players are credited on the album page. A separate published piano score was not found. Year is the single-release year. Disco is used as the genre name; it is not in the taxonomy file.

Second track on Nas's album Illmatic, released 19 April 1994 on Columbia. Produced by DJ Premier (Christopher Martin). The U.S. Copyright Office record for NY state of mind names Nasir Jones and Christopher Martin as authors of words and music, with publication in 1994 on Illmatic. The song uses samples, including Joe Chambers's Mind Rain and Donald Byrd's Flight Time. Year is the album-release year.

songwriter: Kendrick Duckworth, Pharrell Williams, Mark Spears
research_notes: Track on Kendrick Lamar's album To Pimp a Butterfly, released 15 March 2015. Issued as a single on 30 June 2015. Songwriters: Kendrick Duckworth, Pharrell Williams, and Mark Spears. Produced by Pharrell Williams and Sounwave. Year is the album-release year.

Instrumental single by Link Wray & His Ray Men, released 31 March 1958 on Cadence. Wikipedia credits songwriters Milton Grant and Link Wray. The Library of Congress essay describes the 1958 recording and the earlier live improvisation. Year is the release year.

songwriter: Don Felder, Don Henley, Glenn Frey
research_notes: Title song of the Eagles album released 8 December 1976. The single was released 22 February 1977. Music by Don Felder; lyrics by Glenn Frey and Don Henley. BBC Radio 2 credits Frey, Henley, and Felder and gives 1977 as the release year. Year is the single-release year.

Opening track of Slayer's album Reign in Blood, written by Jeff Hanneman, about Josef Mengele's experiments at Auschwitz. The song page and the band's official album page give 7 October 1986. The album Wikipedia page gives 20 October 1986. Year 1986 is consistent. Marked partially verified because the release day differs between sources. The band denied that the song endorsed Nazism.

Instrumental by Larry Heard under the name Mr. Fingers, released in 1986 on the Trax EP Washing Machine. Wikipedia and Discogs agree on Heard as writer and producer and on 1986. Made with a Roland Juno-60 and TR-909. A later vocal mash-up is a different version. Year is the release year.

Traditional Cajun waltz, often called the Cajun national anthem. Wikipedia treats it as traditional. 64 Parishes says it began as a folk melody in French Louisiana and was first recorded by Cajun musicians in 1929. Smithsonian Folkways uses it as a Cajun standard in a lesson. No single author is agreed, so the year is left empty. Spelling varies between Jole Blon and Jolie Blonde. Cajun is not in the taxonomy file.

Recorded by Joe Falcon and Cléoma Breaux on 27 April 1928 in New Orleans for Columbia. Wikipedia and the Library of Congress essay agree. Based on the older tune Jeunes gens campagnard. Described as the first commercial Cajun recording. Year is the recording year.

Hawaiian protest song written in 1893 by Ellen Kehoʻohiwaokalani Wright Prendergast for members of the Royal Hawaiian Band who refused a loyalty oath after the overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani. Also called Mele ʻAi Pōhaku. Wikipedia and the 1993 Hawaiian Journal of History article agree on Prendergast and 1893. Kamehameha Schools dates the composition to 10 February 1893 and says the melody's later history is less certain, including a 1950s setting. Marked partially verified because the melody credit is not settled. Country is United States; region follows the Hawaiian practice used for Aloha ʻOe.

original_format: Electronic dance track with powwow samples
research_notes: Track by Ottawa group A Tribe Called Red, later The Halluci Nation. The Canadian Encyclopedia says DJ Shub (Dan General) sent DJ NDN a song that became Electric Pow Wow Drum. DJ Mag's 5 December 2012 article discusses the track on the group's album. Spotify later dates an album issue to 2013. Year is left empty because 2012 and 2013 both appear. The group describes the style as powwow step.

Comic song written by Mary Travers Bolduc (La Bolduc). English and French Wikipedia agree it was recorded on 6 December 1929 for Starr, with Johnny Monfarleau. The English song page says the record was released in March 1930. Year stored is the recording year. French Wikipedia reports about 10,000 copies sold in the first month; the English song page says 12,000. Chanson québécoise is not a separate taxonomy heading.

original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass | Drums | Piano
research_notes: Lead single from Caifanes' album El nervio del volcán. Spanish Wikipedia says the single was published in May 1994 and credits Saúl Hernández. The English album page gives the single date 17 May 1994 and the album date 29 June 1994, and says all tracks are by Hernández unless noted. Grammy.com discusses the song as the album's lead single. Year is 1994.

Lead single by Natalia Lafourcade, released 6 January 2015, written with Leonel García. English Wikipedia lists the genre as huapango and neofolk. Spanish Wikipedia agrees on the writers and the 6 January 2015 release. Year is the single-release year. Huapango is not in the taxonomy file.

Written by June Carter and Merle Kilgore. Anita Carter recorded it first as (Love's) Ring of Fire. Johnny Cash recorded his version on 25 March 1963 and Columbia released it on 19 April 1963. Wikipedia and the official Johnny Cash site agree on the writers and the 19 April 1963 release. Year is the Cash single-release year.

original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Bass | Drums | Strings
research_notes: B.B. King's recording for Completely Well, released as a single in December 1969. Wikipedia says the song was written by Roy Hawkins and Rick Darnell in 1951, and that early B.B. King releases credited Arthur H. Benson and Dale Pettite. Marked partially verified because of that credit change. Year is the King single year, not the 1951 Hawkins recording.

original_instruments: Piano | Trumpet | Tenor saxophone | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Jazz standard written by Herbie Hancock for his debut album Takin' Off. Recorded 28 May 1962 at Van Gelder Studio; the album was released in 1962 on Blue Note. Hancock plays piano. Wikipedia, the album page, and Hancock's official site agree. Mongo Santamaría's 1963 vocal hit is a later version. Year is the Hancock recording and album year.

songwriter: Al McKay, Allee Willis, Maurice White
research_notes: Single released 18 November 1978, recorded September 1978, from The Best of Earth, Wind & Fire, Vol. 1. Music sequence by Al McKay; lyrics by Allee Willis and Maurice White. Wikipedia, AllMusic, and the Library of Congress essay agree on the writers and 1978. Year is the single-release year.

Gloria Gaynor single released 23 October 1978 on Polydor, from the album Love Tracks. Written and produced by Freddie Perren and Dino Fekaris. It began as the B-side of Substitute. Wikipedia and the Library of Congress essay agree on the writers and the 1978 release. Year is the release year.

Track on Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers), released 9 November 1993, later a single on 31 January 1994. Produced by RZA. Verses by Raekwon and Inspectah Deck; hook by Method Man. Wikipedia credits the song to Wu-Tang Clan. The group's site lists C.R.E.A.M. as track 8 and gives the album date 9 November 1993. The track samples the Charmels' As Long As I've Got You. Year is the album year.

original_instruments: Vocals | Electric guitar | Organ | Piano | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Bob Dylan single released 20 July 1965, recorded 15–16 June 1965 in New York, opening track of Highway 61 Revisited. English Wikipedia, French Wikipedia, and Rolling Stone agree on Dylan as writer and the 20 July 1965 release. Al Kooper played Hammond organ and Paul Griffin piano on the session. A separate published piano score was not found. Year is the single-release year.

Debut single by the Ramones, released February 1976, recorded January 1976, opening track of the album Ramones (23 April 1976). Written by Tommy Ramone and Dee Dee Ramone. Both Wikipedia pages agree. The single title was printed as The Blitzkrieg Bop!!. Year is the single-release year.

Opening track of Megadeth's album Rust in Peace, written by Dave Mustaine. The song page gives the single date 23 September 1990. The album page gives the album date 24 September 1990 and says all tracks are by Mustaine except where noted. Year is 1990.

songwriter: Kevin Saunderson, Paris Grey, Ann Saunderson, Roy Holmon
research_notes: Inner City single released in the UK on 28 November 1988, produced by Kevin Saunderson with vocals by Paris Grey. Wikipedia lists writers Kevin Saunderson, Paris Grey, Ann Saunderson, and Roy Holmon. The Guardian interview with Saunderson and Grey confirms the collaboration and the Detroit-to-Chicago recording. Made with a Casio CZ-5000 and a Roland TR-909. Year is the 1988 single year. The album Paradise followed in 1989.

songwriter: Christopher Wallace, Sean Combs, Jean-Claude Olivier, James Mtume
research_notes: Lead single from Ready to Die. The song page says released 9 August 1994; the album page says 8 August 1994. Writers on the song page: Christopher Wallace, Sean Combs, Jean-Claude Olivier, and James Mtume. Produced by Sean Combs and Poke. It samples Mtume's Juicy Fruit. Album released 13 September 1994. Year 1994 is agreed. Marked partially verified because the single day differs by one day between the two Wikipedia pages.

Written and recorded by Joni Mitchell, released as a Reprise single in April 1970 from Ladies of the Canyon. Her official song page and Rhino agree she wrote it after a trip to Hawaii. Year is the single-release year. This is her second record in the file after Both Sides, Now.

Modern folk song in sea-shanty style written by Stan Rogers, not a traditional shanty. Recorded 23–24 September 1976 and released on Fogarty's Cove in 1976. Wikipedia and a Sudbury.com account of the 1976 Northern Lights Festival agree he wrote it that year. The story of Elcid Barrett is fictional. Year is the album year. Second Rogers song after Northwest Passage.

Lead single from Jagged Little Pill, written by Alanis Morissette and Glen Ballard. The album was released 13 June 1995. The song page gives a US alternative-radio date of 5 June 1995 and lists the single release as 10 July 1995. M Music & Musicians confirms the two writers. Dave Navarro and Flea played guitar and bass on the released track. Year is 1995.

Song by Café Tacvba from the album Re, released 22 July 1994. Written by Emmanuel del Real. Spanish Wikipedia says the single was published in September 1994 and describes it as a norteño parody. The band's site lists La Ingrata as track 2. The English album page agrees on the writer and the 22 July 1994 album date. Year is 1994.

Written and performed by Sidney Simien (Rockin' Sidney). Wikipedia says he included it in October 1984 on My Zydeco Shoes Got the Zydeco Blues, recorded at his home studio in Lake Charles, and that the single was released in 1985. The Grammy site lists the 1986 Best Ethnic or Traditional Folk Recording win for My Toot Toot. Year is the national single year.

Song by Canadian singer k.d. lang, written with Ben Mink, from the album Ingénue (released 17 March 1992). The single was released in the UK on 27 April 1992. Both Wikipedia pages agree. Year is the single-release year.

songwriter: Carly Rae Jepsen, Josh Ramsay, Tavish Crowe
research_notes: Written by Carly Rae Jepsen, Josh Ramsay, and Tavish Crowe. First released in Canada on 20 September 2011 through 604 Records. Wikipedia and MusicBrainz agree on that Canadian date. It began as a folk song and was turned toward pop by Ramsay. Year is the Canadian release year. A wider international release followed in 2012.

songwriter: Miguel Huidobro, Francisco Ayala, Randy Ebright
research_notes: Molotov song written by Miguel Huidobro, Francisco Ayala, and Randy Ebright, produced by Gustavo Santaolalla. English and Spanish Wikipedia agree on the writers. The English song page says released in 2002. The Spanish song page says 4 February 2003. The English album page dates Dance and Dense Denso to 25 February 2003. Year is left empty because the release year is not agreed. The lyric is about racism at the Mexico–United States border.

New song on Zoé's live album MTV Unplugged/Música de fondo, released 22 March 2011, recorded 5 October 2010. Spanish Wikipedia credits the writer as León Larregui. The English album page says all tracks were written by Zoé. Marked partially verified because of that credit difference. Year is the album-release year.

Song by Juan Gabriel about the Noa Noa dance hall in Ciudad Juárez. Included on the album Recuerdos, released 11 March 1980. The Spanish album page credits every track, including El Noa Noa, to Juan Gabriel. BBC Mundo says it was composed in 1979 and included on Recuerdos (1980). A film of the same name followed in 1981. Year is the album year.

Mexican song associated with mariachi and ranchera. English and Spanish Wikipedia and the Los Angeles Times say Rubén Fuentes composed it in 1964. Spanish Wikipedia also records claims that the lyric was written by Imelda Miller or registered to Alejandro F. Roth. Marked partially verified because of that credit dispute. No single original performing artist is fixed here; Fuentes is the reference name.

Traditional son jarocho from the Sotavento region of Veracruz. The Veracruz encyclopedia lists it among the old sones de a montón. Spanish Wikipedia says Lorenzo Barcelata popularized a huapango version using traditional coplas, without a fixed composition date. Smithsonian Folkways includes a recording by Conjunto Alma Jarocha. Year is empty. Son jarocho is already used for La Bamba.

original_format: R&B band with call and response
original_instruments: Vocals | Electric piano | Saxophone | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Written and recorded by Ray Charles. Wikipedia and History.com agree it was recorded at Atlantic in New York on 18 February 1959 and released in June 1959. Charles plays electric piano. The single was split into two parts. A separate published piano score was not found. Year is the release year.

Little Richard single recorded 14 September 1955 at J&M Studio in New Orleans. Wikipedia credits songwriters Dorothy LaBostrie and Little Richard and says Specialty released it in October 1955. The Library of Congress essay also treats it as his 1955 record and describes LaBostrie rewriting the lyric. Richard plays piano on the recording. A separate published piano score was not found. Year is 1955.

Autobiographical country song written by Loretta Lynn. Recorded 1 October 1969 at Bradley's Barn and released as a Decca single on 5 October 1970. Wikipedia and the Library of Congress essay agree. The 1980 film came later. Year is the single-release year.

Traditional North Carolina ballad about Tom Dula, hanged in 1868. The Kingston Trio's Capitol recording became a hit in 1958. The song page credits Alan Lomax and Frank Warner on the commercial issue and says the single was released 19 November 1958. The group page says Capitol issued the single on 8 August 1958. North Carolina DNCR says it hit number one on 19 November 1958. Marked partially verified because the single date and the printed songwriting credit differ from the traditional attribution. Year 1958 is agreed.

Title track of N.W.A's album. English Wikipedia dates the album to 25 January 1989 and says it was recorded in summer and fall 1988. German Wikipedia dates the album to 8 August 1988. The Library of Congress essay calls it a 1988 album and describes verses by Ice Cube, MC Ren, and Eazy-E on the title track. Year is left empty because 1988 and 1989 both appear. The 2015 film of the same name came later.

Outkast single performed, written, and produced by André 3000 (André Benjamin). Released 25 August 2003 from Speakerboxxx/The Love Below, which the album page dates to 23 September 2003. Both pages agree. Year is the single-release year.

Second single from Selena's album Amor Prohibido. Written by Selena Quintanilla-Pérez and Pete Astudillo. English Wikipedia gives the single date 31 July 1994. Spanish Wikipedia says July 1994 and the same writers. Country is United States, as with Como la Flor. Year is 1994. Second Selena record in this file.

original_instruments: Vocals | Guitar | Bass | Drums | Violin | Flute
research_notes: Song by Mi'kmaq and Scottish-Irish singer Willie Dunn, a critique of colonialism. Wikipedia names it as his best-known song and lists a 1973 country-chart single. Discogs lists I Pity the Country on his self-titled Summus album, composed by Dunn, released 6 November 1971 in Canada. CBC Arts also says the song was released in 1971. Year is the album year.

songwriter: Rob Baker, Gordon Downie, Johnny Fay, Paul Langlois, Gord Sinclair
research_notes: Single by The Tragically Hip released in February 1999 from the album Phantom Power (14 July 1998). Songwriters: Rob Baker, Gordon Downie, Johnny Fay, Paul Langlois, and Gord Sinclair. Wikipedia and Universal Music Canada agree on February 1999. Year is the single year. Second Hip song after Ahead by a Century.

Written by Gordon Lightfoot in 1964 and included on his debut album Lightfoot!, recorded in December 1964 and released in January 1966. The song page and the album page agree. Ian and Sylvia released a version in 1965 before Lightfoot's own album. Year is Lightfoot's album year. Second Lightfoot song after The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald.

Ranchera written by Mexican composer Tomás Méndez. English Wikipedia says it was originally released by Chavela Vargas in 1961 on her debut album. Spanish Wikipedia lists Paloma negra among Méndez's works. Year is the Vargas release year. Later uses, including the film Frida, are separate.

original_instruments: Vocals | Accordion | Bajo sexto | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Title song of the Los Tigres del Norte album released 17 June 1997 on Fonovisa. English Wikipedia credits the song to Teodoro Bello. Spanish Wikipedia and the band's site agree on the 17 June 1997 album. Genre on the album pages is norteño. Year is the album year. Second Tigres song after Contrabando y traición. Norteño is not a separate taxonomy heading.

songwriter: Will Butler, Win Butler, Régine Chassagne, Tim Kingsbury, Richard Reed Parry
research_notes: Track on Arcade Fire's album Funeral, released 14 September 2004 on Merge, recorded at Hotel2Tango in Montreal. Issued as a single on 14 November 2005. Songwriters listed as Will Butler, Win Butler, Régine Chassagne, Tim Kingsbury, and Richard Reed Parry. Year is the album year.

title_original: Move On Up a Little Higher
original_format: Gospel vocal with piano and organ
research_notes: Gospel song written by Rev. W. Herbert Brewster. Wikipedia says Brother John Sellers recorded it in late 1946 and Mahalia Jackson recorded it on 12 September 1947 for Apollo, released in December 1947. The Library of Congress essay agrees on Brewster, Jackson, and the 1947 Apollo session. Piano is part of the accompaniment. A separate published piano score was not found. Year is the Jackson recording year.

Written by Billy Steinberg and Tom Kelly and produced by Nile Rodgers. The song page says the single was released on 6 November 1984. The album page lists the single date as 31 October 1984 and the album as 12 November 1984. Year 1984 is agreed. Marked partially verified because the single day differs.

Song by the Quebec band Les Cowboys Fringants, written by Jean-François Pauzé, on the album La Grand-Messe. French Wikipedia and the English album page agree on Pauzé and 2004. The band page dates the album to 23 November 2004. Year is 2004.
